title: A sure million or a long shot?
hook: Take the sure $1M, or gamble for $5M? Then choose again with the sure thing gone.

knows: a felt value that rises more slowly than money can make a sure amount worth more than a gamble (square-root-wealth)
doesNotKnow: that under expected utility, with any felt value that rises with money, a chance both options share cancels out, so two pairs that differ only in that shared chance must get the same answer

misconception: Taking the sure $1M in one pair and the 10% chance of $5M in the other just means I am cautious; some felt value for money fits that.
objective: The learner can explain that removing the 89% both options in a pair share turns pair 1 into pair 2, so expected utility, whatever the felt value, gives the same answer in both, and the sure-then-long-shot pattern fits no felt value.

claims.text: Under expected utility, with any increasing utility function, someone who takes the sure $1M in pair 1 must take the 11% chance of $1M in pair 2 (predict answer A), and 'Expected utility must answer it the same way both times' (reveal, mixed branches).
claims.source: EU(1A) - EU(1B) and EU(2A) - EU(2B) are the same expression, 0.11·u($1M) - 0.10·u($5M) - 0.01·u($0), so 1A over 1B iff 2A over 2B for every u; sweep of 20,058 increasing functions (CRRA, CARA, 20,000 seeded random): all pick the same letter in both pairs, none a mixed pair (node company/domains/briefs/checks/behavioral-allais-certainty-effect.mjs, brief 1 claim 1). Builder statement, not self-verified.

claims.text: 'Take away the 89% each pair shares, and both pairs become 11% of $1M against 10% of $5M.' (reveal, every branch; the toggle 'Take away the shared 89%' greys those 89 cells in all four cards and leaves 11% $1M against 10% $5M and 1% $0 in both pairs.)
claims.source: Pair 1 shares 89% of $1M, pair 2 shares 89% of $0; removing it leaves {11% $1M} against {10% $5M, 1% $0} in both pairs (node company/domains/briefs/checks/behavioral-allais-certainty-effect.mjs, 'Take away the shared 89%' line; brief 1 claim 2). Demo.tsx CARDS lists the shared block first in every card. Builder statement, not self-verified.

claims.text: Matched branches: 1A and 2A fit 'a cautious one, for which $1M is worth more than 10/11 of $5M'; 1B and 2B fit 'a bolder one, for which $5M is worth more than 1.1 times $1M'.
claims.source: With u($0) = 0, 1A (and 2A) iff u($1M) > 10/11·u($5M) = 0.909·u($5M); 1B (and 2B) iff u($5M) > 1.1·u($1M). Witnesses: u = 1 - e^(-3x) picks 1A and 2A (ratio 0.950); u = sqrt(x) picks 1B and 2B (ratio 2.236) (node company/domains/briefs/checks/behavioral-allais-certainty-effect.mjs; brief 1 claim 3). Builder statement, not self-verified.

claims.text: About the learner's own two choices: mixed (1A+2B or 1B+2A) 'no utility function fits your two choices'; matched (1A+2A or 1B+2B) 'one utility function fits your two choices' and 'The sure $1M, then the 10% chance of $5M, would fit none'.
claims.source: Conditional on the learner's two choices, which the reveal reads from the stage state (Demo.tsx p1, p2); all four combinations print in node company/domains/briefs/checks/behavioral-allais-certainty-effect.mjs and follow from claims c1 and c3 (brief 1 claim 4). The walkthrough must show each branch. Builder statement, not self-verified.

claims.text: Names: 'This lean to the sure thing is the certainty effect' (1A+2B); 'Leaning away from the sure thing is the reverse of the certainty effect' (1B+2A, unheld text); 'that is the certainty effect' (matched branches); 'a departure from the model, not a slip'.
claims.source: 'The certainty effect' is the name of the departure from expected utility on these pairs (a term, not an empirical claim about people); brief 1 claim 5; charter company/domains/behavioral.md rule 1 (the reveal says what the model cannot hold, never 'wrong'). Builder statement, not self-verified.

claims.text: HELD (the one type (d) line; mixed branches only). 1A+2B adds 'Re-run with 4,098 people in 19 countries, it held up, weaker than first reported.'; 1B+2A replaces its naming sentence with 'That is the reverse of the certainty effect, which held up with 4,098 people in 19 countries, weaker than first reported.'
claims.source: W-902 row 'Allais / certainty effect' (robust, smaller than the 1979 original; company/research/notes/2026-10-15-w902-behavioral-economics-replication-sourcing.md): Ruggeri et al. 2020 as reported by Cicerale et al. 2022, PLoS ONE, PMC9337702 ('substantially confirmed ... albeit with attenuated effects, in a study enrolling 4098 participants from 19 countries'; opened by research-lead, not by the builder; Ruggeri 2020 itself is not in PMC). Second-hand: whether that is enough is the fact-checker's call. Fallback if not checkable (brief 1): cut the sentence; set HELD_LINE = false in Demo.tsx, which restores the unheld text (1A+2B 75 words, 1B+2A 80 words). The lesson teaches fully without it. Not published until the fact-checker opens it.

claims.text: The four cards: 1A 100% $1M; 1B 10% $5M, 89% $1M, 1% $0; 2A 11% $1M, 89% $0; 2B 10% $5M, 90% $0 (each a 100-cell grid; chances sum to 100%).
claims.source: The lesson's set-up (the Allais common-consequence pairs as given in brief 1); sums checked in node company/domains/briefs/checks/behavioral-allais-certainty-effect.mjs ('probabilities sum to 100%'). Demo.tsx CARDS. Builder statement, not self-verified.

claims.text: Stage gloss: 'Expected utility: any felt value, more is better, weighted by chance.'
claims.source: Definition of the stated model (brief 1 'Stated model': expected utility with any increasing u; P0 condition 1). Wording is the learning designer's 11-word fallback (company/reviews/sure-million-or-long-shot/design.md, open question 1); 'felt value' is the prerequisite lesson's word for utility (economics/square-root-wealth). Builder statement, not self-verified.

claims.text: 'Where it stops: you chose knowing the pairs were linked.' (every branch)
claims.source: About this stage, not other people (charter rule 5, the within-learner cost): both pairs are on screen together, the learner predicts the expected-utility link before choosing, and the toggle links them before the reveal opens (Demo.tsx). Brief 1 reveal text. Builder statement, not self-verified.

claims.text: Hook: 'Take the sure $1M, or gamble for $5M? Then choose again with the sure thing gone.'
claims.source: Describes the set-up: pair 1 offers a sure $1M (1A) or a gamble with a $5M prize (1B); pair 2 has no sure option (2A 11% $1M, 2B 10% $5M). Claim c7. Builder statement, not self-verified.

claims.text: Recall answer: in pair X ($2,000 for sure, or 20% of $3,000, 75% of $2,000, 5% nothing) and pair Y (25% of $2,000, or 20% of $3,000), someone who takes the sure $2,000 must take the 25% chance of $2,000 under expected utility.
claims.source: Taking away the shared 75% of $2,000 turns X into Y; EU(X1) - EU(X2) = EU(Y1) - EU(Y2) = 0.25·u($2k) - 0.20·u($3k) - 0.05·u(0); 20,058 of 20,058 functions agree (node company/domains/briefs/checks/behavioral-allais-certainty-effect.mjs, recall lines; ruling 2 in company/domains/briefs/behavioral.md). Builder statement, not self-verified.

recall.question: Pair X: $2,000 for sure, or 20% of $3,000, 75% of $2,000 and 5% nothing. Pair Y: 25% of $2,000, or 20% of $3,000. Under expected utility, someone who takes the sure $2,000 must choose in Y:
options: Either, depending on how cautious they are
recall.why: Take away the 75% of $2,000 both options in X share, and X becomes Y: 25% of $2,000 against 20% of $3,000 (and 5% nothing). Expected utility must answer both pairs the same way, so the sure $2,000 goes with the 25% chance.
